title: TB0-06689
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXXXX, the claimant, alleges he is a citizen of the People's Republic of China (PRC). He claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA).

The claimant alleges that in 2007 he was suffering from chronic stomach problems. Despite medical intervention the claimant's medical condition did not improve. In XXX 2008, the claimant was introduced to the practice of Falun Gong as a means to address his health problems. The claimant began practicing at home and noticed an improvement in his health. In XXXXXX 2008, the claimant joined his cousin's underground Falun Gong group practice.

The claimant alleges that on XXXXXXX, 2009, the claimant's group practice was raided by members of the Public Security Bureau (PSB). The XXXX members of the group including the claimant were arrested and detained. The claimant's stomach ailment returned and his health deteriorated while in custody. On XXXXXX, 2010, the claimant was released on a 10,000 RMB bond so that he could obtain medical treatment with the added conditions that he regularly report to the PSB. While on bail, the claimant's medical condition improved. Recognizing that he would soon return to detention, he left China with the assistance of a smuggler and arrived in Canada on XXXXX, 2010. The claimant alleges that when he failed to report to the PSB as scheduled, the PSB attended his home to locate him. He further learned that the PSB issued a summons for him. He alleges that the members of his Falun Gong group are still being incarcerated.
The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The reasons are as follows.

The determinative issue in this claim is the credibility of the claimant's testimony concerning his practice of Falun Gong and his pursuit by authorities in China based on illegal Falun Gong activities. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has not been a credible witnesses in regard. The reasons for these findings are noted below.
The claimant established his identity as a national of the People's Republic of China, with his household register booklet or Hukou and Resident Identity Card.2 CREDIBILITY

In assessing credibility, the panel was mindful of the claimant's age, education, and background. The claimant alleges he has 9 years of formal education and that he was a XXXXX in China. The panel is also mindful that the claimant testified that he is attending English as a second language classes in Canada and notes that the claimant understood and responded to some of the panel's questions in English and without the aid of translation. In addition, the panel is cognizant of the many difficulties faced by a claimant in establishing a claim, including cultural factors, the milieu of the hearing room, and the stress inherent in responding to oral questions through an interpreter and nervousness. Arrest of Fellow Church Members and Pursuit of Claimant by the PSB

The claimant alleges that he and six other members of his Falun Gong group were arrested and detained. He alleges that he gained temporary release from detention on bail to seek medical attention. He further alleges while on bail he was able to leave China and travel to Canada. The claimant alleges that all the members of his group received multi-year sentences and that the PSB are in pursuit of him.

The claimant tendered into evidence the summons3 that he has alleged was left with his parents after he failed to report to the PSB as directed. The documentary evidence4 notes that a summons would almost always be issued to the individual rather than a household or family member. However, it was also noted that it is very common in China for the police authorities to leave the summons with family members, instructing them to pass it along to the person named on the summons. The person accepting the summons would be expected to sign an acknowledgment of receipt. Though this is not actually the proper procedure it happens all the time, especially in cases when a person in the summons is not easily locatable The documentary evidence5 states that there are two types of summonses in China including: Zuanhuan summons is considered a non-coercive measure and is used when no arrest or detention of suspects is contemplated or necessary or when cooperation is expected or flight is not likely; and, Juzhuan summons which is translated as an Arrest-Summon (for Interrogation) summons. This summons is considered a coercive measure and is used when voluntary compliance is not appropriate or when the Zuanhuan summons has failed. The claimant's testimony is that he had already been arrested but that he was on bail due to medical reasons. He insisted the PSB were intent on arresting him and that they have been to his home on 7 occasions searching for him. He testified that they last attended his home in XXXXXX, 2011 in pursuit of him. Given the claimant's allegation that he had previously been incarcerated with the XXXX members of his Falun Gong group and that the police were intent on arresting him, it is reasonable to expect that the PSB would have issued a Juzhuan summons (Arrest-Summon for Interrogation).

The documentary evidence6 also notes the format and appearance of summonses. It is stated that the notice is prepared in triplicate. The original is kept at the police station, the duplicate copy is signed, dated and returned by the suspect and one copy is left with the suspect. The documentary evidence provided an example of the Juzhuan summons from Fujian Province where the claimant is from and notes the information that is to be included on the portion of a summons left with the person or family members of the person named in the summons. It states that the summons should include, among other things, the following statement: According to PRC Criminal Procedure Law Article 45, it has been decided that investigator from this bureau (name) will effectuate arrest at the resident (address) of (named person).

The documentary evidence also notes that the summons would include the date issued and the date on which the summons was served on the person and the person's signature. The summons tendered by the claimant does not contain his address nor is the date of service indicated. The summons also does not bear the signature of the claimant's parents despite his testimony that they were the persons on whom the summons was served. The summons also does not bear the statement "according to PRC Criminal Law Procedure Article 45".

The panel also that the summons tendered by the claimant does not conform to either of the examples of summonses in the country condition documents. In fact, the summons tendered by the claimant bears reference to section 83 of the "Security Management Law of the People's Republic of China rather than sections 45 or 92 of the PRC Criminal Procedure Law.

In addition, there is no mention on the summons of the claimant's alleged violation of bail. It is reasonable to expect that given the claimant had failed to honour his bail conditions by failing to report to the PSB that the summons would reflect that in some way. The panel notes from the documentary evidence that fraudulent documents including summonses are easily acquired in China. I have considered the inconsistencies in the summons provided by the claimant compared to the documentary evidence, as well as the ease with which one can get fraudulent documents in China and I find on a balance of probabilities that the summons provided by the claimant is not a genuine document. The panel further finds the tendering of a fraudulent document in support of his claim undermines the claimant overall credibility. Bail Decision Letter and Receipt

The claimant tendered a bail decision letter together with a receipt for payment of his bond as corroboration of his allegation that he had been arrested and incarcerated for his Falun Gong activities. The panel notes that the receipt tendered indicates that the receipt was provided for payment of a fine for illegal Falun Gong activities and not for payment of a bond. The receipt states, "Being Fined for join illegal Falun Gong and Cult." (sic) The bail decision letter makes it clear that the claimant was to be released on bail upon the payment of the 10,000 RMB bond and that the money would not be confiscated unless the claimant failed to comply with the conditions of his bail. The claimant was unable to provide an explanation for the discrepancy. The panel finds that these two documents contradict one another and as such both documents are rendered suspect. In this regard, the panel draws a negative inference. The panel has considered the inconsistencies in the documents provided by the claimant and further considered that the claimant has tendered a fraudulent summons in support of his claim as well as the ease with which one can get fraudulent documents in China and I find on a balance of probabilities that the bail decision letter and receipt provided by the claimant are not genuine documents. Travel to Canada

The claimant alleged that he used the services of a smuggler to leave China and travel to Canada because he was being pursued by the PSB. The claimant alleged that he was provided a false passport by the smuggler. The claimant was asked what information the smuggler provided him concerning his false identity in the event he was asked questions by officials during transit. The claimant testified that he was only told the name that was in his passport and told to follow the smuggler and not worry. The claimant testified that the passport was written in English and that he could not read the contents. He acknowledged that he did not know if the passport contained his date of birth or it is had been previously used by to exit or enter any other countries. The claimant testified that he was posing as a resident of the United Kingdom but stated that he was not provided his fraudulent address in the U.K. The claimant further testified that he did not know the name that the smuggler was using in his passport despite his testimony that they were traveling together and posing as uncle and nephew. While the panel does recognize the need for the Board to be sensitive to the vulnerabilities of claimants traveling under false documents, it does not excuse the claimant for his lack of knowledge of the identity he and the smuggler were traveling under. The panel finds it neither plausible nor credible that the claimant would not be aware of this basic information in the face of the obvious likelihood that he would be questioned about it in transit. The Claimant's Family in China

The claimant testified that his family in China has not suffered any consequences as a result of his participation in Falun Gong and failure to surrender to the police. Country documentary evidence7 regarding Falun Gong states that it is considered a cult by the Chinese government and is banned and, indicates that Chinese authorities use the family of absconding practitioners as hostages to force the practitioner to give up the practice. If a practitioner does not cooperate with the authorities, the family is subject to punishment as well, including harassment, arbitrary interrogation, losing a job, and losing housing benefits. The claimant's testimony is that the only "threat" that the family received was they would be punished if they were found to be withholding information about the location of the claimant. In the context of this case, given the seriousness of the accusations, and where the absconding person has not returned for 18 months, and as alleged by the claimant, the PSB are still looking for him as late as XXXXXX of 2011, it is reasonable to assume that his family would have experienced some greater sanctions in an effort to have the claimant turn himself in to the PSB. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's family continuing ability to carry on with their normal lives without facing consequences or more rigorous interrogation at the hands of the PSB. Lack of Persuasive Evidence to Corroborate Residency in China at Material Time

In order to corroborate his residency in China, the claimant tendered a number of original documents, including a Resident Identity Card (RIC), a Household registry (Hukou), medical records as well as his Bail decision letter and receipt. However, the panel finds that the documents provided by the claimant fail to provide pervasive corroborative evidence that he resided in China at the time of the alleged raid. The claimant's RIC and his Hukou were issued in 2002 and provide no corroboration that the claimant was living in China after 2002. Having previously found that the bail decision letter and receipt are not genuine documents, they too do not provide corroboration that the claimant was in China at the material time.

The claimant was asked why he had not produced additional work documents to establish his residency in China in 2009. The claimant alleges that no such work records are available because he was paid cash. The panel rejects the claimant's explanation. The claimant was reminded that he was provided a screening form by the Board which specifically requested that he provide evidence of his work and residency in China. The claimant made no effort to obtain any work documents despite being requested through the screening form. In addition, the claimant is represented by competent counsel and the importance of obtaining these documents is evident. Furthermore, the claimant alleges that he worked at the same company for ten years. It is reasonable to expect that he would have some documentation to demonstrate that he worked at the company. Unfortunately, as a result, there is no persuasive evidence to corroborate that the claimant was in China at the time he alleges he was being pursued by the PSB. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's failure to obtain work records or other persuasive records to establish he was in China at the material times.

The claimant tendered two medical booklets to corroborate his illness. The medical documents are from two different hospitals. One booklet provides information on the claimant's treatment for his alleged stomach ailment from XXXXXX 2007 to XXXXXX 2008. The second booklet provides information on the treatment of the claimant's stomach ailment from XXXXX 2010 to XXXX 2010. The panel notes that neither of the documents contains any other information with regard to the health of claimant other than his alleged stomach ailment as would reasonably be expected. Further, the panel notes that neither of the documents contains a hospital chop or seal nor do they contain any security feature to establish their provenance. In addition, I have considered that the claimant has tendered fraudulent documents in support of his claim as well as the ease with which one can get fraudulent documents in China and I find on a balance of probabilities that the medical booklets provided by the claimant are not genuine documents.

Based on the foregoing cumulative negative credibility findings and negative inferences drawn above, and, the lack of persuasive evidence, the panel finds that the claimant's testimony, that his Falun Group in China was raided and that he is being pursued by the PSB is not credible. Knowledge of Falun Gong

In general, the claimant's understanding of the Falun Gong was fairly well developed. The claimant alleges that while in China he had been practicing Falun Gong in a group once a week and practicing on his own every day. Since being in Canada, the claimant testified that he continues to practice in a group. He alleges that since he has arrived in Canada he has completely read the book Zhuan Falun several times. As such, it is reasonable to expect that he would have a good understanding of the practice of Falun Gong and would be able to describe the practice accurately. As such, the panel gives no weight to the claimant's ability to answer questions about Falun Gong.

While it is difficult to make a judgment regarding the genuineness of a claimant's beliefs it is necessary in this case. In doing so, the panel considered the totality of the evidence available. Although it is true the claimant does possess some knowledge of Falun Gong it does not necessarily mean he is a genuine practitioner. Merely having some information regarding basic teachings and practice or the lack of such information does not necessarily reflect genuine or false practice. It is necessary to consider the totality of evidence available to the panel. The claimant provided three letters of support from his fellow practitioners in Canada. However none of the letters corroborate when the claimant began practicing Falun Gong in Canada. The claimant arrived in Canada in XXXX 2010 and alleged that he began to practice in a group within weeks. However two of the letters he tendered state that author met the claimant in XXXXX 2010 while practicing Falun Gong. The third letter does not identify when the author first met the claimant. The claimant has alleged he fled China because he was being persecuted for his Falun Gong practices. He further alleged that the practice of Falun Gong was so important to him that he risked his personal safety and security to practice it in China. As such, it is reasonable to expect that the claimant would resume practice in Canada at his first opportunity. Further, the genuineness of the claimant's Falun Gong practice is central to the claimant's claim. It is reasonable to expect that he would provide corroboration that he resumed his Falun Gong practice shortly after arriving in Canada. The panel notes that the claimant is represented by experienced counsel and the importance of providing this corroboration is evident. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's failure to provide corroboration that he resumed his group practice of Falun Gong shortly after arriving in Canada.

The claimant also tendered photographs of his participation in group Falun Gong activities including participation in demonstrations XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. The claimant also testified that he was XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXX. The claimant testified that he XXXXXXXXXXXXXX "Falun Gong is good." The claimant further testified that other XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX made disparaging remarks about the Chinese government's treatment of practitioners of Falun Gong. The panel was only provided with "XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX however the panel was not provided with a translation of the alleged XXXX. As such, the panel can put little weight on this evidence.

In any event, these documents and the claimant's testimony can only attest to the claimant's participation in Falun Gong activities; they do not attest to his motivation. In this regard, recent case law8 indicates that a pastor's assessment of the genuineness of a person's faith cannot be substituted for the assessment that the panel is required to make. In the same regard, the panel finds that the assessment a Falun Gong practitioner cannot be substituted for the assessment the panel is required to make. The panel gives little evidentiary weight to these documents.

The panel does note however, that some of the photographs tendered by the claimant are of the claimant joining a demonstration XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX in Toronto. In addition, the claimant testified that since XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX he is more at risk because the Chinese authorities will identify him. The claimant was asked during the hearing why he would take such a risk of demonstrating at the XXXXX given that he did not know what the outcome of his refugee claim would be. The claimant responded that he believed it was the right thing to do and that he did not think it was a risk because the "Master would protect" him. The panel asked the claimant why he would risk sanctions being taken out against his parents because of his actions in Canada. The claimant testified that it was important to get the truth out about Falun Gong and he believed that the Master would protect him and his parents. The panel rejects the claimant's testimony. The claimant had the opportunity in China to practice Falun Gong openly as means of protest against the Chinese government's treatment of Falun Gong, however, he chose to practice in secret to avoid the repercussion of the PSB. The claimant's actions in China tend to undermine his testimony that the "Master" would protect him. Given the claimant's alleged treatment by Chinese authorities because of his Falun Gong practice and in context that the claimant could not anticipate the outcome of his refugee claim hearing, the panel finds it unreasonable that he would create circumstances which would further endanger him and his family. In this regard the panel draws a negative inference.

Having previously found that the claimant's Falun Gong group practice was not raided and that he is not being pursued by the PSB, and in the context of all of the findings noted above, the panel finds that the claimant was not a genuine practitioner in China as he alleges. The panel further finds, on a balance of probabilities, and on the basis of the findings and negative inferences noted above, and in the context of his knowledge of Falun Gong, that the claimant's allegation that he was a genuine Falun Gong practitioner in China is not credible and was only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent claim.

Having found that the claimant was not a Falun Gong practitioner in China, the panel must consider whether the claimant is a genuine Falun Gong practitioner in this county. The panel finds it reasonable to expect 'good faith' in making a refugee claim. In this regard, R.P.G. Haines, the Chairman of a refugee status appeal panel and A.G. Wang Heed, a member of the United Nations High Commission for Refugees stated in part: If there is no good faith requirement in the sur place situation, it places in the hands of the appellant for refugee status the means of unilaterally determining the grant to him or her of refugee status.9

In this regard, the panel cites the following from James Hathaway's The Law of Refugee Status with regard to "sur place" claims: An individual who as a stratagem deliberately manipulates circumstances to create a real chance of persecution which did not exist cannot be said to belong to this category.10 The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities that the claimant deliberately created circumstances to increase his jeopardy of persecution. As such, the panel finds on a balance of probability, that this claim has not been made in good faith.

Having found that the claimant was not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner in China and having found that this claim has not been made in good faith, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, and in the context of findings noted above, that the claimant began Falun Gong activities in Canada only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent refugee claim.

In the context as noted above, as well as in the context of the cumulative findings and negative inferences noted above, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner nor would he be perceived to be in China.

On the basis of the totality of the evidence and the cumulative findings, the panel finds that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted or that he would be personally subjected to a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture by any authority in the People's Republic of China.

The claimant is neither Convention refugees nor a person in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division rejects his claim. (signed) "L. Favreau" L.
